faqs.question: How much does it cost to enter the Valley of the Kings?
faqs.answer: The general entry ticket for foreign adults costs approximately 750 EGP and includes access to three tombs (excluding certain premium tombs). Foreign students pay around 375 EGP. Egyptian nationals pay a much lower local rate. There is also a small additional tram fee, around 20 EGP, to reach the tombs from the visitor center.

faqs.question: Does the ticket include Tutankhamun's tomb?
faqs.answer: No, Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) requires a separate ticket, priced at around 700 EGP for foreign adults, in addition to the general entrance ticket.

faqs.question: How many tombs can I visit with one ticket?
faqs.answer: The standard general admission ticket includes entry to three tombs, chosen from those currently open to the public. Premium tombs such as Tutankhamun's and Seti I's require additional, separately priced tickets.

faqs.question: What are the opening hours of the Valley of the Kings?
faqs.answer: The valley is typically open from around 6:00 am to 5:00 pm, with hours occasionally extending slightly during summer months.

faqs.question: Why is Tutankhamun's tomb so famous?
faqs.answer: Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) is renowned because it was discovered by Howard Carter in 1922 almost completely intact, unlike nearly every other tomb in the valley, which had been looted by robbers in antiquity. It yielded an extraordinary collection of treasures, now largely displayed at the Grand Egyptian Museum.

faqs.question: How many tombs are there in the Valley of the Kings?
faqs.answer: There are 63 known numbered tombs and chambers, designated KV1 through KV63, ranging from small pits to elaborate multi-chambered royal tombs.

faqs.question: Which is the largest tomb in the valley?
faqs.answer: KV5, built for the sons of Ramesses II, is the largest known tomb in the valley, with over 120 identified chambers.

faqs.question: Are all the tombs open to the public?
faqs.answer: No, only a rotating selection of tombs is open at any given time. Authorities periodically close and reopen different tombs to manage visitor numbers and allow humidity-sensitive ancient wall paintings to recover.

faqs.question: Is photography allowed inside the tombs?
faqs.answer: Photography rules have varied over time and can differ by tomb; some allow standard photography while others restrict it or require a paid permit. It's best to check current signage and rules at the ticket office before entering.

faqs.question: How do I get to the Valley of the Kings from Luxor?
faqs.answer: The valley is on the West Bank of the Nile, roughly a 25–30 minute drive from Luxor Temple on the East Bank, typically reached by car, taxi, or organized tour after crossing the Nile bridge.

faqs.question: How long does a visit to the Valley of the Kings take?
faqs.answer: Most visitors spend 2 to 3 hours visiting three or four tombs, plus travel time on the tram from the visitor center to the tomb entrances.

faqs.question: Is the Valley of the Kings hot to visit?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is an exposed desert valley with little shade, and tomb interiors are not air-conditioned. Visiting early in the morning, especially outside the summer months, is strongly recommended.

faqs.question: Can I buy Valley of the Kings tickets online in advance?
faqs.answer: Yes, tickets can generally be purchased through the official Egyptian antiquities ticketing portal or at the on-site ticket office; booking through a licensed tour operator is another common option.

faqs.question: Is the Valley of the Kings wheelchair accessible?
faqs.answer: Accessibility is limited. The desert terrain is uneven, and most tomb entrances involve descending ramps or steps into narrow corridors, making full wheelchair access difficult for most tombs.

faqs.question: What other sites are near the Valley of the Kings?
faqs.answer: Nearby West Bank sites include the Temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari, the Valley of the Queens, the Colossi of Memnon, and the ancient workers' village of Deir el-Medina, all commonly combined into a single West Bank tour.
